editorial.headline: Education Support, with a Crucial Bali Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the services around education itself—and remains nationally open to foreign ownership, subject to a decisive Bali risk-and-scope assessment.
editorial.body:
Education is not only delivered in classrooms. This activity covers the supporting work that helps education systems function: education consulting; vocational, career and academic guidance; educational evaluation and testing; student-exchange programmes; curriculum development; and specialist or rehabilitative work assessing learning ability. It also includes operational advice and assistance for the education sector. Within the non-formal route, it encompasses institutions run through cooperation between an accredited or recognised foreign educational institution and an Indonesian educational institution, in accordance with applicable requirements.

The registration can therefore suit organisations whose role is advisory, evaluative, developmental or programme-based rather than conventional teaching. It is open across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, giving the activity a broad practical range—from a small specialist guidance practice to a larger organisation administering educational services or exchange programmes. The scope matters: a business should describe the actual service it intends to provide with care, because the code brings together several forms of non-teaching educational support.

Nationally, the position is clear. The activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Bali is more exacting. The province permanently blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities island-wide. For this activity, the Bali outcome depends on the precise scope declared: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is low for some scopes and higher for others. PMA registration in Bali is available only where the business declares the applicable higher-risk scope, and the exact activity should be verified in live OSS before proceeding.

That distinction is not a technical footnote. A national foreign-ownership position does not, by itself, settle the Bali registration outcome. The practical question is whether the real educational-support activity falls within the higher-risk scope required for PMA registration there. Founders should treat the scope declaration as the central regulatory description of the business, not as an administrative afterthought.
